utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Will the Registrar call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Case Number IT-99-37-PT, the Prosecutor versus Milan Milutinovic, Nikola Sainovic, and Dragoljub Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Appearances. INTERPRETER: Microphone for Mr. Nice, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry. I appear for the Prosecution with Cristina Romano, Patricia Fikirini, and Susan Grogan as the case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Eugene O'Sullivan appearing for Mr. Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Toma Fila and Mr. Vladimir Petrovic on behalf of Nikola Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Tomislav Visnjic and Peter Robinson for General Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a Status Conference. We have a number of matters to get through. I'll begin with the pending motion, the application for binding orders filed by the Ojdanic Defence team. We will be scheduling a hearing in this matter as soon as the Trial Chamber is fully constituted. That will be in another three to four weeks. There is the Ojdanic motion challenging jurisdiction. I understand that the Appeals Chamber will issue a decision in this matter very soon. I turn to disclosure of witness statements. Rule 66(A)(i) statements disclosure complete for all three accused, and the same for 66(A)(ii) statements, with the exception of one witness in respect of whom protective measures have been ordered. All expert reports have been disclosed in both B/C/S and in English. I turn now to Rule 68 disclosure, and we should go into private session since we will be dealing with a Rule 70 matter.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I was saying, Mr. Nice, that I understand that there is a wider problem of disclosure relating to the implementation of what is called the e-disclosure system. And it is now being said that this is working to the prejudice of the Defence. It is said that little, if any, material relating to Kosovo is available on this system. What is the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: First of all, there's a one-side paper distributed to Defence counsel and available for Your Honour that sets out the present position. Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That was distributed just now, was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not sure when it was distributed to counsel, but just now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's dated the 10th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. It sets out what the system is. It sets out the means of accessing the system which can be done via a password, and I have no doubt that if at any stage the Bench or any of its members would like to have it demonstrated to see how easy it is of access, that could be arranged. But of course, you need a password, so you can't just enter the site that's given here. Under the heading "general collections," we see a reference to the 4.700.500 pages of material all of which is being assessed for inclusion in the system. Of that some 35 per cent or 1.6 million pages are already on the system with a further nearly 0.4 million pages in final stages of preparation, and they should be on the system within one month. There are then 900.000 pages being inspected visually, and it's forecast that they will be on the system by the summer recess. So by that stage, some 55 per cent of the collections will be available electronically to the Defence. The remaining 1.8 approximately million pages form part of the restricted collections, principally, I suppose, witness materials or witness-related materials and Rule 70 and other confidential material. As you see from the note, a review of some 640.000 pages of Rule 70 material is underway to check to what extent some of that material may have had its Rule 70 status lifted. And once that exercise is completed, any material free of Rule 70 restrictions can then be added to the electronic system. And a final review of witness-related materials is planned to see if there is material that can be placed on the electronic system perhaps in a redacted form. So that's the general state of the electronic disclosure system. And it's obviously an enormous project, and a very considerable advance to the benefit of all parties, but particularly to the Defence, on what was done before under any manual system. Turning then to case-specific disclosures, the system has the capability of delivering documents on a trial-specific basis, and indices will be available to trial teams and are then intended to replace CD sets that have been provided. And overall, it's felt that the advantages are improved, search efficiency for the Defence and simpler tracking of what has been provided without there being a need for substantial paper-storage requirements for the Defence. It also obviously accelerates the speed in which material can be provided. So far as this case is concerned, as the Court may recall, some 29 CD-ROMs of material were disclosed in October of last year. They will be added to the electronic system by June of this year, the first week it's hoped, so that they will then be searchable by the same search tools as operate on the system generally. That's a summary of where we are. The OTP staff member in charge or, for these purposes, in charge of this system is available within the building today. And I think following the proceedings, should you require his attendance here to assist further, but I hope that you'll be satisfied with what I have been able to explain to you here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [No microphone].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. One way or another. At the moment they've got their 29 CD-ROMs. Those CD-ROMs will, or the content of those CD-ROMs will be loaded on to the general system by the first week of June and comprise then part of the 35-odd per cent of our material that's searchable on that system. And as we see, there's more material going to be provided to the system by the summer recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So this state of accessibility has only been reached just now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Comparatively recently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Recently. All right, thank you. Mr. O'Sullivan, do you have anything to say on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm grateful to Mr. Nice for providing us with this document which does shed some light on this question for us. We would be grateful to know when the case-specific disclosures to the Kosovo collection will be in this system. That's the -- as I understand this document, there are three divisions that Mr. Nice has referred to. 55 per cent of this general collection will be on line by the summer recess. Then there's the 45 per cent which apparently is going to remain restricted, which is fine. But it's the case specific to the Kosovo collection that we are most interested in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Obviously, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: -- which appears not -- there are no dates surrounding the case-specific Kosovo collection. That's the one we're most interested in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, Mr. O'Sullivan is naturally concerned about the Kosovo case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Our understanding is that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My apologies. Our understanding is that this material which they have already had in the 29 CD-ROMs will be available on the system certainly by the summer recess, and the CD-ROMs themselves will be loaded by June of this year, by the first week of June of this year. And of course, the endpoint of the exercise is when all the material that isn't sensitive so that it can't be loaded on to a publicly available system has been provided. And I think the expectation broadly is that would all be accomplished by the summer recess, but I'll be corrected if I'm wrong on that. So in short, they have got the material in CD-ROM. That material is going to be on the system by the first week of June. And all the material, subject to that which has to be withheld, should be available by the summer recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By the way, sorry -- I haven't checked this with Mr. O'Sullivan, but we understand from the records that we have got that Mr. O'Sullivan has yet to open his account. I'm not sure if that's right, and to seek to gain access to the system. It may be that we're wrong on that. It appears that his password hasn't yet been used. He may benefit from trying it out. But it may be he hasn't done -- maybe we are wrong on that; I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I haven't, but my co-counsel has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. Perhaps he's as electronically challenged as I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we hesitate to say anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Rule 66(B) disclosure. The Milutinovic Defence has requested access under Rule 66(B) to various confidential materials from the Milosevic trial. There's no reciprocal disclosure any more. And are you in a position to say whether -- have you received that request and what is the response to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We haven't received any formal request yet. So we await it in writing, and we will deal with it when it comes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes. Disclosure from the Milosevic trial, arrangements are in place with the Registry for the Defence teams to obtain access to public material. And I understand that this arrangement appears to be working. Agreed and adjudicated facts, discussions have commenced, although slowly, on 17 items proposed by the Sainovic Defence. And the Defence provided the Prosecution yesterday with a revised list based on those discussions. Any comments on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't know if Your Honour's had an opportunity to look at the 14 points --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then I think perhaps Your Honour should at some stage. We suspect that they are points that may not be contentious and may be admitted, such matters as Mr. Sainovic's date of birth and his history of positions held and so on, much of which is in the public domain. And indeed, we find at item 10 a proposition to the effect that the Autonomous Region of Kosovo and the Metohija is located at the south part of the Republic of Serbia which we suspect is a proposition we may find it in our ability to admit. What we find more concerning is that there is nothing that going to be truly time-saving on the indictment that's contained here and that this document effectively leaves us exactly where we are without any effective admissions. We've gone through various processes in this trial, and indeed I think in others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, the question is whether it represents a bona fide and a best-effort on the part of the Sainovic Defence. Let me ask Mr. Fila. Or is it --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in keeping with the instructions received from you and pursuant to the manner and methodology in a number of cases before this International Tribunal, on two occasions we did compile, first of all 17, and the second time 14 facts as our proposals for hearing the Prosecution's stand on. And so that in that domain, what would be the subject of proof in a limited way that this should be brought down to a narrow spectrum of questions and problems. Our first attempt was made in January this year, but it did not come upon the understanding of the Prosecution. We tried in a serious manner to open up and broach topics that we consider to be important for the Defence case of Mr. Nikola Sainovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, I'm sorry to interrupt you. The 17 facts represent the totality of what you're able to offer?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is precisely what I wish to clear up. In the first letter, we offered 17 facts. In the second letter, which was sent to our learned colleagues the day before yesterday, we have an additional 14 facts listed. And in total, in the two letters, we have put forward 31 facts. Now, if there is understanding on their part, then we shall continue the process. This is a first step, an initial attempt, and if it comes upon understanding, on the basis of what has been done so far, we are, of course, ready to take the next step in conformity with the instructions given by you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, well I expect both parties to continue working. Of course, you understand, Mr. Petrovic, if you list as a fact or if you offer as a fact a matter such as the date of birth of your client, you know, some questions may be raised about your bona fides. I expect the exercise to be conducted in good faith, and I expect a best effort from both parties in this exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is with regret that I have to notice that with a certain amount of sarcasm which this example was quoted by my colleague, that is just part of one fact which is incorporated in the indictment, and therefore it was for this reason that it was found in our text. Of course, the text itself does contain far more serious topics and proposals compared to the date of birth of Mr. Sainovic. Of course, that is not challenged or contested. But as that is in the indictment as well, then that is the first part or part 1 of fact 1. Of course, that is not the substance and crux of the matter. That lies, the crux lies in other proposals. And as I emphasise, this is the beginning of a process, and there are things that are relevant there for Your Honour when it comes to decision making on the charges contained in the indictment. And I should also like to stress that the substance and essence of what the proposal, the second proposal made up of 14 facts is, is that it is along the lines of everything that has been done thus far with the other two accused; that is to say, Mr. Milutinovic, and Mr. Ojdanic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. We still are working with an estimate of 100 to 120 witnesses. And I don't know whether the original estimate of three to four months would still stand. I very much doubt that. There's the matter of the health of Mr. Milutinovic. Private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are we back in open session? Yes. I was asking whether there was any other matter that counsel would wish to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, yesterday at our 65 ter conference, I sent you a message. And I could repeat that message if you haven't received it, or if you have received it and don't wish to hear it again, that would be fine, too. But I would like to at least confirm that items I mentioned yesterday with respect to the resources of the Ojdanic team has come to your attention and hopefully something can be done about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I would like you to make the points so that they can be on record so that I can take the necessary steps that are feasible to have them addressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. And I won't take too much time with this, but it's of extreme importance to General Ojdanic and his Defence team. I understand that the Pre-Trial Judge has a duty to prepare the case for trial so that on the first day of trial we are prepared to proceed. And unfortunately, on the first day of trial in this case, as things now stand, we won't be prepared to proceed. As you know, the Ojdanic team has received no compensation for its work since April of 2003. And by the time this trial is to commence, it may be one or two years without any compensation for the Defence of General Ojdanic. As a result of that, we will not be in a position to make any admissions, stipulations, any agreements to experts because we will not have had an opportunity to conduct any investigation into those matters. We'll be completely unprepared to make an opening statement because there will be in excess of 300.000 pages of disclosure which we will not have read and have conducted no meaningful investigation. We will be in no position to cross-examine the first witness or any other witness because we haven't read the material, haven't investigated it, and haven't prepared. At the beginning of the trial when our payments would then commence, because it's a new phase, we would probably need at least six months of full-time preparation by myself and Mr. Visnjic before we could be in a position to begin the trial. If the Trial Chamber declines to give us time to prepare, I think we would be in no -- have no alternative than to move to withdraw from representing General Ojdanic, and I know that my own bar rules do not allow me to render ineffective assistance to a client, and I would be completely unable to render effective assistance to General Ojdanic with the resources that have been allotted to us by the Registry. Even if we were not allowed to withdraw, I can tell you that General Ojdanic would fire us, and he would be prepared to represent himself if it was necessary without adequate resources for his Defence. What is not an option, and I would like to make this very clear, is that somehow the lawyers would go along and be there as some kind of puppets for a show that ask a few questions, make a few objections, and not really be effective advocates for our client. That's completely unacceptable to us, and we would not allow ourselves to be used in that way. So I'm saying this now to you on the 12th of May of 2004 in the hope that that situation on the first day of trial and thereafter can be avoided. The Appeals Chamber has said that the issue of equality of arms doesn't arise until the trial, and so we have no remedy against the Registrar's decision before then. We have tried, as you know, we have been up to the Appeals Chamber on this issue. We have sent more than 12 letters to the Registrar. And it's our hope that you, as the Pre-Trial Judge, would have the foresight to manage this problem before it comes to trial. It's easy to say that it's a matter for the Registry, but the Chambers and the Registry have to work together to ensure that trials occur when they're ready, and when they do occur, they're fair. And I can tell you that General Ojdanic will not receive a fair trial unless somebody becomes proactive and manages this problem. I thank you for your patience. I'm happy to answer any questions you may have. But I want to make it very clear to you what is the situation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: On what basis are you now working?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: General Ojdanic's lawyers are completely pro bono at this time. We have tried to push the train that is out of gas, but manually and do a few things to keep General Ojdanic supplied with materials and do the minimum amount of things that need to be done. But basically, we're operating on a completely volunteer basis and have been since April 2003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, as you know, we have to operate within the framework of the Rules governing the Tribunal. The Appeals Chamber has ruled on the issue which you raised concerning costs. That decision obviously has to be respected. I listened carefully to what you said, and I read the 65 ter statement yesterday. And you have to be careful how you couch your representations. And I would like to think that the representations do not constitute a threat to the Chamber, because the Chamber, of course, and the Tribunal does not operate under threats from counsel or from any body. So I take it that the remarks are made entirely in good faith and on the basis of your understanding of the duties that you have to your client. I see it as a public issue and a public-interest issue. And for that reason, I am going to raise it with the President and the Bureau of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Judge Robinson. I assure it's not a threat, but I think a very clear picture of the reality if nothing is done. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. The only other business, then, would be, before I call on the three accused persons, to say that the next Status Conference will be Wednesday, the 8th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Arising from the point that Mr. Robinson has been making, the following: Although, it's of course essentially a matter between Defence counsel, the Registry, and Your Honour, the Prosecution and its witnesses have an interest, a very direct interest, in not finding themselves here at court on the first day of any trial with witnesses prepared only to face an abandonment or postponement of the case that has been forecast and might have been avoided. So we have to a significant interest a real interest. Thinking on that and seeking to assist the Chamber, I raise as an issue for consideration this: To what extent is it right for counsel to take the case to the position of the first day of the trial if they know that on that day they will either withdraw or be sacked? If they do know that's the position, subject to what they follow from Your Honour's steps which you may take with the president, if they know that is their position, may their duty not be to act earlier so that the trial won't be compromised at the last day. That's all I offer, and I offer it bearing in mind that the Prosecution has a real and substantial interest in not having the trial aborted at the very last minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I acknowledge the interest of the Prosecution in this matter. And I consider your remarks to be very pertinent. Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. And I also acknowledge the right of the Prosecution to be concerned, and we would, of course, appreciate their support in this situation because they, too, have an interest in seeing that there's an effective Defence. I would simply, in addressing what Mr. Nice has said, refer everyone to the Appeals Chamber decision which appears to indicate that we are not allowed to withdraw during the pre-trial phase and our duty is to do the best we can with the limited resources that we have. And that's what we have been doing. But those resources are very, very much underestimated for this case. And we will not be able to be in a position to be prepared to offer an effective defence at trial unless something is changed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. May I then ask the three accused persons whether they have anything to say in relation to the conditions of their detention or anything else relating to the trial. First, Mr. Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. Do you have anything to say?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And Mr. Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED OJDANIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I do. Your Honour, it has been more than two years since the law on cooperation with The Hague Tribunal was adopted by my country. As soon as the law was passed, I, as an accused, arrived before this Tribunal respecting that law. From then to this day, I have not spent more than five minutes of the court's time. Therefore, I now ask your leave to speak for about 3 minutes about the conditions that I find deeply distressing. First of all, the fact that among the accused there are people who honourably, professionally, and morally, and with high ethical standards defended their country and its territorial integrity, but those who for years, not to say, decades have been planning, organising, ordering, or personally committing horrendous crimes on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija are ethnically cleansing Kosovo and Metohija of Serbs and other non-Albanians are not here. In their documents of 1999, among other terrible things, in the political declaration, they say that the Liberation Army of Kosovo started this war under the slogan "either Kosovo will be ours or it will all be reduced to dust and ashes." I wish to believe that this great injustice, in my view, will soon be corrected. Secondly, I have come before this Tribunal, and I am ready to answer before this Tribunal or anybody else as to what I did and how I did it. As a soldier and as a human being, I am proud of the fact in which I fulfilled the vow I made to my people and my homeland. I'm also happy because I feel completely not guilty, and I can look anyone on this planet in the eye. Thank you for allowing me to speak. I do not wish to repeat what my Defence counsel, Mr. Robinson, has said. But I entreat Your Honour to do your very best to make sure that my Defence and others' Defence is not subservient to the work of the Prosecution, which every day feeds us hundreds and thousands of hundreds of exculpatory and other material, and rightly so. It would really be a sin for a person to be convicted here because someone has not approved sufficient funds for a proper Defence. To be quite honest, I cannot look them in the eye, but I am doing my very best as far as I'm able to help my counsel so that they can prepare as best they can. Thank you. And I apologise if I have overstepped my time that I asked you for. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ojdanic. Mr. Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED SAINOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you. I have nothing to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There being no other matters, the hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: at 3.15 p.m.
